overview: Black fianchettoes the queen's bishop on b7 before White has committed the c-pawn, and usually follows with ...e6. White can transpose to the Queen's Indian with c4 or play a London-style 3.Bf4 and e3, or 3.g3 and Bg2. Black aims to control e4 and keep a solid, flexible position, while White tries to take space in the centre. Without White's c4 there is no real Queen's Indian theory.

white_ideas.idea: Bf4, e3, h3, Nbd2 and c3, London set-up, or c4 for a Queen's Indian
g3, Bg2 and O-O with queenside expansion

black_ideas.idea: ...Bb7, ...e6 and ...Be7, control of e4 with a solid fianchetto
Strike with ...c5 or ...d5 depending on White's set-up

typical_structures.structure: Queen's Indian-style Black fianchetto against d4/e3 or d4/c4

character.notes: Solid, flexible with few weaknesses; Black is hard to break down.

structure.notes: Centre not committed, d4/e3 against ...e6/...d5 or ...c5: flexible.

approach.notes: A move order Black uses against many White set-ups, but it is a normal Indian line: standard.

level.notes: Plans are clear but need judgement; little theory.

sublines_that_differ.name: Neo-Queen's Indian: 3.Bf4
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. Nf3 b6 3. Bf4 Bb7 4. e3 e6

character.reason: Compact Queen's Indian structure, few ways to lose quickly.

approach.reason: Played at all levels, not a one-move-fits-all system.

plans.reason: Black's bishop on b7 on the long diagonal.
